High-rise window views: Evaluating the physiological and psychological
impacts of green, blue, and built environments
Mohamed Elsadeka,b,*, Zhang Deshuna,**, Binyi Liuc,***
aDepartment of Landscape Architecture, College of Architecture and Urban Planning, Tongji University, Shanghai, 200092, China

A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: A growing body of research indicates that visual exposure to nature can enhance mental well-being. However,

Visual contact knowledge gap, we utilized aerial drone-captured videos taken from a height of 90 m to present comprehensive

Window view
included three key elements: built structures, greenery, and water bodies. Forty-five participants were randomly
Anxiety
Mental health assigned to view six conditions in a laboratory setting. Physio-psychological responses to each condition were
Human perception measured using a portable electroencephalogram device, which continuously recorded brainwaves, and Ergo-
LAB, which monitored heart rate variability. Additionally, participants completed anxiety level assessments and
subjective feelings questionnaires. Our findings revealed that visual contact with all window views produced
significantly greater positive effects compared to viewing control or built environments. Among the window
views, those featuring green space with water or green space alone elicited the most beneficial outcomes,
including increased alpha brainwave activity, enhanced parasympathetic nervous system activation, heightened
levels of relaxation and comfort, and lower anxiety levels. The study’s findings indicate that high-rise building
residents can benefit from 4-min exposure to greenery, either with water or alone, through window views, in
promoting mental health. The study emphasizes the importance of considering window views in urban high-rise
planning and design to enhance the mental health and well-being of city dwellers.

4. Discussion
The global surge in high-rise constructions prompts critical inquiries
into their impact on resident well-being, highlighting the need to un-
derstand psycho-physiological responses to high-rise living. Our study
aims to address this gap by meticulously investigating the influence of
high-rise window views, positioned at a height of 90 m, featuring
greenery space, water, and buildings on individuals’ well-being. In

4.1. Window view and physiological well-being
4.1.1. Alpha relative power
The occipital lobe, the brain’s primary visual processing area, hosts
the brain’s fundamental "resting rhythm" known as the alpha brainwave
rhythm. This rhythm, prominent during relaxed wakefulness, plays a
crucial role in visual processing and attention [46]. Our study found that
the relative power of alpha waves varied significantly with different
visual stimuli. Viewing scenes that included greenery (G), greenery with
water (GW), water alone (W), or combinations thereof significantly
enhanced alpha wave activity compared to control (C) or building-only
(B) views. This suggests greater relaxation when participants observed
natural elements, a finding supported by previous research associating
